Isothermal means the temperature stays fixed throughout, so the gas has to keep exchanging heat with its surroundings to balance out the work done. Adiabatic on the other hand has no heat transfer at all, Q is zero, so if the gas does work its internal energy and temperature actually drop.

In an adiabatic process the system is basically sealed off thermally, no heat in or out, so all the work comes at the cost of internal energy and temp changes. Isothermal is opposite, temp is held constant by letting heat flow in/out as needed.

the way i remember it is isothermal = slow process with T constant and heat flowing to keep it that way, adiabatic = fast/insulated process where no heat can escape so T changes. also on a pV graph the adiabatic curve falls more steeply than isothermal because gamma > 1.

PV = constant for isothermal but for adiabatic its PV^gamma = constant, and since gamma is bigger than 1 the adiabatic curve is steeper. That steepness comes from the fact that adiabatic has no heat exchange so temperature is not being held fixed like in isothermal.

Honestly the core difference is just heat exchange - isothermal allows it (thats literally how T stays same) while adiabatic completely blocks it. As a result adiabatic expansion cools the gas down since energy for work comes from within.

If u insulate a container so no heat gets in/out, thats adiabatic, and temperature will rise or fall depending on compression/expansion. Isothermal needs a good conductor wall or very slow process so heat keeps flowing and T doesnt change, and its pV curve is less steep than adiabatic's.

so basically these are two extremes - one where the system is in perfect thermal contact with environment (isothermal, T const) and one where its totally isolated thermally (adiabatic, Q=0). in the second case work done by/on gas directly changes its internal energy hence temp changes.

Adiabatic process has Q=0 by definition, meaning the container walls dont let any heat pass, and because of that the temperature isnt constant - it varies as the gas expands or compresses. Isothermal is the reverse case, heat is exchanged freely so T is constant, and if u plot both on same pV diagram the isothermal line is more gradual compared to adiabatic.
